html:
A herding culture of the steppes north of the Black and Caspian seas, from about 3300 to 2600 BCE. The map shows it in 3000 BCE. Its people buried their dead in pits under earth mounds called kurgans, often sprinkled with red ochre.

The Yamnaya lived mostly from cattle and sheep, moving with ox-drawn wagons, and they probably rode horses, building on the domestication of the horse on the steppe. Many scholars think they spoke Proto-Indo-European, the ancestor of languages from Irish to Hindi.

Ancient DNA has revealed a huge Yamnaya expansion. From about 3000 BCE their descendants spread west into Europe, where they formed the Corded Ware culture and contributed to the Bell Beaker peoples, and east to the Altai. A large share of the ancestry of living Europeans, and a smaller share in South Asia, goes back to steppe herders like them. On the steppe itself they were followed by the Catacomb culture and later the Sintashta and Andronovo cultures.
